stem: A financial services company stores trade records as objects in a new Amazon S3 bucket. An application uploads thousands of records each day. The company must retain each record in an immutable form for 7 years. No user, including the root user, can be allowed to delete or overwrite a record before the end of its retention period. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: retain each record in an immutable form

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, and change the application so that every upload request sets compliance mode and a retain-until date 7 years ahead.
options.why: It works, but changing the application to set [a unique retention period for individual objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-retention-per-object-or-bucket-default) is more work than a bucket default.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, change the application so that every upload sets governance mode and a 7-year retain-until date, and let only the security team bypass it.
options.why: Governance mode stops users [unless they have special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode), so the security team can still delete, and the application change adds work.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in compliance mode, and set a default retention period of 7 years that applies to every new object version.
options.why: In compliance mode a version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), and the bucket default sets [how long to protect every object version](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention) without code.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in governance mode, set a default retention period of 7 years, and allow only the security team to bypass governance retention.
options.why: In governance mode, users cannot delete a locked version [unless they have special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode), so the security team could still delete records.

explanation: The deciding phrase is the root user. In compliance mode a locked version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), and [its retention period can't be shortened](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode). A bucket default retention sets [how long to protect every object version](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention) that arrives later, so the application needs no change.
takeaway: Not even the root user can delete: use Object Lock compliance mode with a bucket default retention.
twin: If the stem said "the security team must be able to remove the protection when a legal request requires it" instead: governance mode with the bypass permission, because it protects versions [unless they have special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode).
say: Even the root user can't delete in compliance mode, and a bucket default covers every new record.

stem: A financial services company stores trade records as objects in a new Amazon S3 bucket. An application uploads thousands of records each day. The company must retain each record in an immutable form for 7 years. Most users must not be able to delete or overwrite a record, but the security team must be able to remove the protection when a legal request requires it. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the security team must be able to remove the protection
retain each record in an immutable form

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, and change the application so that every upload request sets compliance mode and a retain-until date 7 years ahead.
options.why: Every upload sets compliance mode, and a version in that mode [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), so the security team is locked out as well.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, change the application so that every upload sets governance mode and a 7-year retain-until date, and let only the security team bypass it.
options.why: It works, but changing the application to set [a unique retention period for individual objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-retention-per-object-or-bucket-default) is more work than a bucket default.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in compliance mode, and set a default retention period of 7 years that applies to every new object version.
options.why: A version in compliance mode [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), so the security team cannot remove the protection for a legal request.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in governance mode, set a default retention period of 7 years, and allow only the security team to bypass governance retention.
options.why: Governance mode stops most users, and a user with [s3:BypassGovernanceRetention](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) can remove the protection, so the security team alone gets that permission.

explanation: AWS says to use governance mode when [some users with special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-mode-choice) can alter the retention or delete objects. A user who holds [s3:BypassGovernanceRetention](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) and sends the [x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) header can remove the protection. The bucket default sets [how long to protect every object version](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention), so the application needs no change.
takeaway: When a privileged team needs to remove the lock, use governance mode and give that team the bypass permission.
twin: If the stem said "No user, including the root user, can be allowed to delete or overwrite a record" instead: compliance mode, because a version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode).
say: Governance mode stops most users, and the bypass permission lets the security team remove the lock.

stem: A company receives order files from partners in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each new file must start a processing job. The processing team runs workers that read from an existing Amazon SQS FIFO queue, and the team will not change the workers. The company wants to decouple the upload side from the processing side and does not need S3 to keep events in order. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: an existing Amazon SQS FIFO queue

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification for object-created events that sends each event directly to the SQS FIFO queue as its destination.
options.why: An SQS FIFO queue is not a valid notification destination: [FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues aren't supported](../facts/s3.md#s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations).

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function, and write code in the function that sends each event to the SQS FIFO queue.
options.why: It works, but the Lambda function is code to write and maintain, and an EventBridge rule reaches the FIFO queue without code.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EventBridge delivery for the bucket, and create an EventBridge rule that matches object-created events and targets the SQS FIFO queue.
options.why: With EventBridge delivery, [all events are sent to EventBridge](../facts/s3.md#s3-eventbridge-all-events-more-targets), and a rule can [route events to additional targets](../facts/s3.md#s3-eventbridge-all-events-more-targets) such as the FIFO queue, with no code.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that lists the bucket every minute, finds the new files, and sends a message to the SQS FIFO queue for each one.
options.why: It works, but polling needs custom code and repeated list requests, and it reacts later than an event rule that fires for each new object.
options.misconception: polls the bucket for new objects instead of reacting to events

explanation: S3 event notifications cannot target the queue, because [FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues aren't supported](../facts/s3.md#s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations). For that case AWS says [you can use Amazon EventBridge](../facts/s3.md#s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations). EventBridge receives every event of the bucket, and a rule with the FIFO queue as its target forwards the object-created events. The setup is configuration, with no function to write.
takeaway: S3 events for an SQS FIFO queue go through Amazon EventBridge and a rule.
twin: If the stem said "an existing Amazon SQS standard queue" instead: an S3 event notification sent directly to the queue, because events can go to [Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-events-destinations).
say: S3 can't notify a FIFO queue directly, so I'd turn on EventBridge and add a rule that targets the queue.
